Ibn al-Mundhir related from him regarding ﴿al-mursalat 'urfa﴾ that he said: the angels; ﴿fa'l-fariqat farqa﴾: the angels, who separated truth from falsehood; ﴿fa'l-mulqiyat dhikra﴾: with the revelation.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "Woe" (wayl) is a valley in Hell in which the pus of the people of the Fire flows, and it was made for the deniers.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿minma'in mahin﴾ that he said: weak.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding kifatan that he said: a shelter (kinnan).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also regarding ﴿rawasi shamikhat﴾ that he said: towering mountains; and regarding His saying "furatan" that he said: sweet.

This is Surah 77 (al-Mursalat), verses 1–28 (part 1 of 2), from al-Shawkani's Fath al-Qadir.

It is Meccan according to al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Ata' and Jabir.
Qatadah said: except for one verse of it, which is His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down﴾. That verse is Medinan. This is also reported from Ibn Abbas.

Al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "The Surah al-Mursalat was revealed at Makkah."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud who said: "While we were with the Prophet ﷺ in a cave at Mina, the Surah al-Mursalat was revealed, 'urfan (in succession). He was reciting it, and I was receiving it from his mouth, and his mouth was moist with it, when a snake sprang upon us. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Kill it!' We rushed at it, but it escaped. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'It has been protected from your evil, just as you have been protected from its evil.'"

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Ibn Abbas that Umm al-Fadl heard him reciting: ﴿By those sent forth in succession﴾, and she said: "O my son, you have reminded me by your recitation of this Surah. It was the last thing I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recite in the Maghrib (prayer)."

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

His saying: ﴿By those sent forth in succession﴾. The majority of the exegetes said: they are the winds. It was also said they are the angels; this is the view of Muqatil, Abu Salih and al-Kalbi. It was also said they are the prophets.

According to the first view, Allah, glorified is He, swore by the winds sent forth by His command, as in His saying: ﴿And We sent the winds fertilizing﴾ [al-Hijr: 22] and His saying: "He sends the winds," and other such verses.

According to the second view, He swore by the angels sent forth with His revelation, command and prohibition.

According to the third view, He swore by His messengers sent to His servants to convey His laws.

The accusative of ('urfan) may be: either as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), meaning "sent forth for the sake of 'urf," which is the opposite of nukr (denial/disapproval), and from it is the poet's saying:
"Whoever does good, his reward will not be lost; the 'urf does not vanish between Allah and people."
Or it may be a circumstantial accusative (hal) with the meaning of "consecutive," one following another like the mane of a horse (ka-'urf al-faras). The Arabs say: "The people went to so-and-so 'urfan wahidan" when they headed toward him, and "they were against so-and-so like the mane of the hyena" when they gathered against him. Or it may be an infinitive (masdar), as if he said: "and those sent forth sending," i.e., consecutively. Or it may be accusative by removal of the preposition, i.e., "and those sent forth with 'urf."

The majority read 'urfan with a sukun on the ra'. 'Isa ibn Umar read it with a damma. It was also said that what is meant by "those sent forth" is the clouds, because of the blessing and punishment in them.

﴿Then those that blow violently﴾, which are the winds that blow strongly.

Al-Qurtubi said, without disagreement: one says "'asafa bi-l-shay'" when he destroys and ruins it, and "naqah 'usuf" means a she-camel that carries its rider swiftly, speeding along like the wind. One also says "'asafat al-harb bi-l-qawm" when war carries them off. It was also said they are the angels entrusted with the winds, driving them. It was also said they drive away the soul of the disbeliever. It was also said they are the destroying signs, such as earthquakes and the like.

﴿And those that spread widely﴾: meaning the winds that bring the rain, spreading out the clouds widely. Or the angels entrusted with the clouds, who spread them out, or who spread their wings in the air at the descent with the revelation. Or they are the rains, because they spread vegetation.

Al-Dahhak said: he means what is spread out of books and the deeds of the children of Adam.

Al-Rabi' said: it is the Resurrection for the Last Day, by the spreading of souls. The waw is used here because it begins another oath.

﴿Then those that separate, separating﴾: meaning the angels who bring what distinguishes between truth and falsehood, and between the lawful and the unlawful.

Mujahid said: it is the wind that separates the clouds, scattering them. It is reported from him that they are the verses of the Qur'an that distinguish between truth and falsehood. It was also said they are the messengers, who separated what Allah commanded from what He forbade. This is the view of al-Hasan.

﴿Then those that deliver a reminder﴾: they are the angels.

Al-Qurtubi said: by consensus; that is, they deliver the revelation to the prophets. It was also said it is Jibril, and he was named with the plural form out of honor for him. It was also said they are the messengers who deliver to their peoples what Allah revealed to them; this was said by Qutrub.

The majority read ("fa-l-mulqiyati") with a sukun on the lam and a light qaf, as an active participle. Ibn Abbas read it with a fatha on the lam and a shadda on the qaf, from talqiyah, which is the conveying of speech to the addressee. The more probable view is that the first three are for the winds, and the fourth and fifth are for the angels. This is the view chosen by al-Zajjaj, al-Qadi and others.

﴿As an excuse or a warning﴾: their accusative is either as a substitution (badal) for dhikran, or as an object. The governing element for both is the nunated verbal noun, as in His saying: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger an orphan﴾ [al-Balad: 14–15]. Or it is an object of purpose: i.e., for excuse and warning. Or it is a circumstantial accusative by the known interpretation: i.e., making excuse or warning.

The majority read the dhal in both with a sukun.

Zayd ibn Thabit and his son Kharijah ibn Zayd, and Talhah, read them with a damma.

Al-Haramayn (Ibn Kathir and Nafi') and Ibn Amir and Abu Bakr read them with a sukun in ('udhran) and a damma in (nudhuran).

The majority read ﴿'udhran aw nudhran﴾ with the conjunction "aw" (or).

Ibrahim al-Taymi and Qatadah read it with the conjunction "wa" (and), without an alif. The meaning is that the angels deliver the revelation as an excuse from Allah to His creation and as a warning of His punishment. Thus said al-Farra'. It was also said: an excuse for the righteous and a warning for the falsifiers.

Abu Ali al-Farisi said: it is possible that ('udhur) and (nudhur) with the heavy form are plurals of 'adhir and nadhir, as in His saying: ﴿This is a warner of the warners of old﴾ [al-Najm: 56]. Then it would be accusative as a circumstantial element of the delivering: i.e., they deliver the reminder in the state of excuse and warning. Or they are two objects of (dhikran): i.e., remember excuse or warning.

Al-Mubarrad said: both in the heavy form are plurals, and the singular is 'adhir and nadhir.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the answer to the oath, saying: ﴿Indeed, what you are promised will surely occur﴾, i.e., what you are promised of the coming of the Hour and the Resurrection is certain to happen.

Then He, glorified is He, explained when that will occur, saying: ﴿So when the stars are obliterated﴾, i.e., their light is erased and their brightness departs. One says "tamasa al-shay'" when it is effaced and its trace disappears.

﴿And when the sky is split open﴾, i.e., it is opened and cleft. Similar is His saying: ﴿And the sky will be opened and will become gates﴾ [al-Naba': 19].

﴿And when the mountains are blown away﴾, i.e., they are uprooted from their places swiftly. One says "nasafta al-shay'" and "ansaftuhu" when you take it swiftly.

Al-Kalbi said: they are leveled with the earth. The Arabs say: "The she-camel nasafat the pasture," when she grazes it. It was also said: they are made like grain which is winnowed with a winnowing shovel. Similar is His saying: ﴿And the mountains will be crumbled to dust﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 5]. The first view is preferable.

Al-Mubarrad said: nusifat means they are uprooted from their places.

﴿And when the messengers are brought to their appointed time﴾. The hamza in (uqqitat) is a substitution for a damma waw, and every waw that takes a damma where the damma is inherent may be replaced by a hamza. Abu 'Amr, Shaybah and al-A'raj read it with a waw, and the rest read it with a hamza. Al-waqt is the term at which a thing that is deferred to it occurs. The meaning: a time was set for them for the separation and judgment between them and their nations, as in His saying: ﴿On the day when Allah gathers the messengers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 109]. It was also said this refers to this world: i.e., the messengers were gathered for their appointed time which had been set for sending down punishment upon those who denied them. The first view is preferable. Abu Ali al-Farisi said: i.e., He made the Day of Judgment and the Separation a time for them. It was also said: they were sent at known times according to what Allah knows.

﴿For what day were they deferred?﴾ This interrogative is for magnification and wonder: i.e., for what great day, at which the servants marvel because of its severity and the abundance of its terrors, has a term been set for their gathering? The clause is a quoted saying of an implied verb, which is the answer to (idha), or it is in the place of an accusative as a circumstantial element of the pronoun in (uqqitat). Al-Zajjaj said: the purpose of this appointing is to clarify the time at which they will attend to bear witness against their nations.

Then He explained this day, saying: ﴿For the Day of Separation﴾. Qatadah said: on it people will be separated by their deeds, to Paradise and to the Fire.

Then He magnified that day, saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Separation is?﴾, i.e., what will inform you of the Day of Separation? He means it is a wondrous, awesome matter whose measure cannot be grasped. "Ma" is the subject and "adraka" its predicate, or the reverse, as Sibawayh preferred.

Then He mentioned the condition of those who denied that day, saying: ﴿Woe on that day to the deniers!﴾, i.e., woe to them on that awesome day. "Waylun" is originally a masdar that takes the place of its verb, and it was changed to the nominative to indicate permanence. "Al-wayl" means destruction, or it is the name of a valley in Hell. He repeated this verse in this Surah because He divided the woe among them according to the measure of their denial, for each denier of a thing has a punishment in addition to his denial of another thing, and some thing denied is greater in sin than denial of another, so he receives from the woe in proportion to that denial.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned what He did to the disbelievers of the earlier nations, saying: ﴿Did We not destroy the former peoples?﴾ He, glorified is He, informed of the destruction of the disbelievers of the past nations from the time of Adam to Muhammad ﷺ.

Muqatil said: he means by punishment in this world when they denied their messengers.

﴿Then We follow them with the later ones﴾, i.e., the disbelievers of Makkah and those who agreed with them when they denied Muhammad ﷺ.

The majority read (nutbi'uhumu) with a damma, as a resumption: i.e., then We follow them.

Abu al-Baqa' said: it is not conjoined, because conjunction would require the meaning: "We destroyed the former ones, then We followed them with the latter ones in destruction." That is not the case, because the destruction of the later ones has not yet occurred.

What indicates the damma is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, "thumma sanutbi'uhumu." Al-A'raj and al-Abbas from Abu 'Amr read "nutbi'hum" with a jazm, as a conjunction to "nuhlik." Shihab al-Din said: on the basis that the verb is conjoined to the whole clause "Did We not destroy."

﴿Thus do We deal with the criminals﴾: i.e., like that terrible act, We will do with them. He means whoever We destroy later on. The kaf is in the position of an accusative as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, i.e., We will do with every polytheist a destruction like that destruction, either in this world or in the Hereafter.

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers!﴾, i.e., woe on the day of that destruction to those who denied the Books of Allah and His messengers. It was said the first woe is for the punishment of the Hereafter, and this one is for the punishment of this world.

﴿Did We not create you from a despised fluid?﴾, i.e., weak and contemptible, which is the sperm drop.

﴿Then We placed it in a secure place﴾, i.e., a safe place, which is the womb.

﴿For a known period﴾, i.e., until a known measure, which is the duration of pregnancy. It was also said: until it is formed.

(Then We determined.) The majority read "faqadarna" with a light dal. Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read it with a shadda, from taqdir. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: they are two dialects with the same meaning. One says "qadartu kadha" and "qaddartuhu." ﴿So how excellent are We as determiners!﴾, i.e., how excellent are We as the determiners. It was said the meaning is: We determined it short or long. It was also said the meaning of "qadarna" is "Our dominion."

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers!﴾ — for denying Our power over that.

Then He explained to them the wondrousness of His making and the greatness of His power, so that they might take heed, saying: ﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle﴾. The meaning of "kifat" in the language is gathering and collecting; one says "kafata al-shay'" when he gathers and collects it, and from this a saddlebag and a pot are called "kafat." The meaning: Have We not made the earth a container for the living upon its back and the dead in its belly, gathering and collecting them?

al-Farra' said: He means it gathers them alive upon its back in their houses and dwellings, and gathers them dead in its belly, i.e., takes them into possession, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿alive and dead﴾. Sibawayh recited:
"Noble when the vipers gather into their holes from the frost."

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "kifatan" means receptacles, and from it is the poet's saying:
"You are today alive above the earth, and tomorrow you will be gathered into the kifat."
i.e., into a grave. It was also said the meaning of making it kifat is that what comes out of a human of waste is buried in it.

Al-Akhfash and Abu 'Ubaydah said: "the living and the dead" are two attributes of the earth: i.e., the earth is divided into the living, which is what grows, and the dead, which is what does not grow.

Al-Farra' said: The accusative of ﴿أحياءً وأمواتًا﴾ ("living and dead") is due to the verb "gathering" (kifat) governing it. That is, "Did We not make the earth a gatherer (kifat) of the living and the dead?" If it is read with tanwin, what follows it is put in the accusative. It was also said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the earth, meaning: from it such-and-such, and from it such-and-such. It was also said that it is a verbal noun (masdar) described by it for emphasis.

Al-Akhfash said: kifatan is the plural of kafitah, and "the earth" is intended as a collective, so it is described with a plural adjective.

Al-Khalil said: At-takaffut (the act of gathering) is turning a thing over, back to belly or belly to back. It is said: "The people withdrew (inkafatat) to their dwellings," meaning they went away.

﴿And We placed in it firm mountains (rawasi shamikhat)﴾, that is, tall mountains. Ar-rawasi are the firmly fixed ones, and ash-shamikhat are the tall ones; every high thing is shamikh. ﴿And We gave you to drink sweet water (furat)﴾, that is, sweet water. Al-furat is sweet water from which one drinks and with which one irrigates.

Muqatil said: All of this is more wondrous than the resurrection.

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾, for the blessings We bestowed upon them, among Our blessings of which this is a part.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, related from Abu Hurayrah regarding ﴿And those sent forth in succession (al-mursalat 'urfa)﴾ that he said: They are the angels, sent with goodness (al-'urf).

Ibn Jarir related the same from Ibn Mas'ud.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿al-mursalat 'urfa﴾ that he said: the wind; ﴿fa'l-'asifat 'asfa﴾: the wind; ﴿wa'l-nashirat nashra﴾: the wind.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from him regarding ﴿al-mursalat 'urfa﴾ that he said: the angels; ﴿fa'l-fariqat farqa﴾: the angels, who separated truth from falsehood; ﴿fa'l-mulqiyat dhikra﴾: with the revelation.

﴿And when the messengers are brought to their appointed time﴾. The hamza in (uqqitat) is a substitution for a damma waw, and every waw that takes a damma where the damma is inherent may be replaced by a hamza. Abu 'Amr, Shaybah and al-A'raj read it with a waw, and the rest read it with a hamza. Al-waqt is the term at which a thing that is deferred to it occurs. The meaning: a time was set for them for the separation and judgment between them and their nations, as in His saying: ﴿On the day when Allah gathers the messengers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 109]. It was also said this refers to this world: i.e., the messengers were gathered for their appointed time which had been set for sending down punishment upon those who denied them. The first view is preferable. Abu Ali al-Farisi said: i.e., He made the Day of Judgment and the Separation a time for them. It was also said: they were sent at known times according to what Allah knows.

﴿For what day were they deferred?﴾ This interrogative is for magnification and wonder: i.e., for what great day, at which the servants marvel because of its severity and the abundance of its terrors, has a term been set for their gathering? The clause is a quoted saying of an implied verb, which is the answer to (idha), or it is in the place of an accusative as a circumstantial element of the pronoun in (uqqitat). Al-Zajjaj said: the purpose of this appointing is to clarify the time at which they will attend to bear witness against their nations.

Then He explained this day, saying: ﴿For the Day of Separation﴾. Qatadah said: on it people will be separated by their deeds, to Paradise and to the Fire.

Then He magnified that day, saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Separation is?﴾, i.e., what will inform you of the Day of Separation? He means it is a wondrous, awesome matter whose measure cannot be grasped. "Ma" is the subject and "adraka" its predicate, or the reverse, as Sibawayh preferred.

Then He mentioned the condition of those who denied that day, saying: ﴿Woe on that day to the deniers!﴾, i.e., woe to them on that awesome day. "Waylun" is originally a masdar that takes the place of its verb, and it was changed to the nominative to indicate permanence. "Al-wayl" means destruction, or it is the name of a valley in Hell. He repeated this verse in this Surah because He divided the woe among them according to the measure of their denial, for each denier of a thing has a punishment in addition to his denial of another thing, and some thing denied is greater in sin than denial of another, so he receives from the woe in proportion to that denial.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned what He did to the disbelievers of the earlier nations, saying: ﴿Did We not destroy the former peoples?﴾ He, glorified is He, informed of the destruction of the disbelievers of the past nations from the time of Adam to Muhammad ﷺ.

Muqatil said: he means by punishment in this world when they denied their messengers.

﴿Then We follow them with the later ones﴾, i.e., the disbelievers of Makkah and those who agreed with them when they denied Muhammad ﷺ.

The majority read (nutbi'uhumu) with a damma, as a resumption: i.e., then We follow them.

Abu al-Baqa' said: it is not conjoined, because conjunction would require the meaning: "We destroyed the former ones, then We followed them with the latter ones in destruction." That is not the case, because the destruction of the later ones has not yet occurred.

What indicates the damma is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, "thumma sanutbi'uhumu." Al-A'raj and al-Abbas from Abu 'Amr read "nutbi'hum" with a jazm, as a conjunction to "nuhlik." Shihab al-Din said: on the basis that the verb is conjoined to the whole clause "Did We not destroy."

﴿Thus do We deal with the criminals﴾: i.e., like that terrible act, We will do with them. He means whoever We destroy later on. The kaf is in the position of an accusative as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, i.e., We will do with every polytheist a destruction like that destruction, either in this world or in the Hereafter.

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers!﴾, i.e., woe on the day of that destruction to those who denied the Books of Allah and His messengers. It was said the first woe is for the punishment of the Hereafter, and this one is for the punishment of this world.

﴿Did We not create you from a despised fluid?﴾, i.e., weak and contemptible, which is the sperm drop.

﴿Then We placed it in a secure place﴾, i.e., a safe place, which is the womb.

﴿For a known period﴾, i.e., until a known measure, which is the duration of pregnancy. It was also said: until it is formed.

(Then We determined.) The majority read "faqadarna" with a light dal. Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read it with a shadda, from taqdir. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: they are two dialects with the same meaning. One says "qadartu kadha" and "qaddartuhu." ﴿So how excellent are We as determiners!﴾, i.e., how excellent are We as the determiners. It was said the meaning is: We determined it short or long. It was also said the meaning of "qadarna" is "Our dominion."

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers!﴾ — for denying Our power over that.

Then He explained to them the wondrousness of His making and the greatness of His power, so that they might take heed, saying: ﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle﴾. The meaning of "kifat" in the language is gathering and collecting; one says "kafata al-shay'" when he gathers and collects it, and from this a saddlebag and a pot are called "kafat." The meaning: Have We not made the earth a container for the living upon its back and the dead in its belly, gathering and collecting them?

al-Farra' said: He means it gathers them alive upon its back in their houses and dwellings, and gathers them dead in its belly, i.e., takes them into possession, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿alive and dead﴾. Sibawayh recited:
"Noble when the vipers gather into their holes from the frost."

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "kifatan" means receptacles, and from it is the poet's saying:
"You are today alive above the earth, and tomorrow you will be gathered into the kifat."
i.e., into a grave. It was also said the meaning of making it kifat is that what comes out of a human of waste is buried in it.

Al-Akhfash and Abu 'Ubaydah said: "the living and the dead" are two attributes of the earth: i.e., the earth is divided into the living, which is what grows, and the dead, which is what does not grow.

Al-Farra' said: The accusative of ﴿أحياءً وأمواتًا﴾ ("living and dead") is due to the verb "gathering" (kifat) governing it. That is, "Did We not make the earth a gatherer (kifat) of the living and the dead?" If it is read with tanwin, what follows it is put in the accusative. It was also said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the earth, meaning: from it such-and-such, and from it such-and-such. It was also said that it is a verbal noun (masdar) described by it for emphasis.

Al-Akhfash said: kifatan is the plural of kafitah, and "the earth" is intended as a collective, so it is described with a plural adjective.

Al-Khalil said: At-takaffut (the act of gathering) is turning a thing over, back to belly or belly to back. It is said: "The people withdrew (inkafatat) to their dwellings," meaning they went away.

﴿And We placed in it firm mountains (rawasi shamikhat)﴾, that is, tall mountains. Ar-rawasi are the firmly fixed ones, and ash-shamikhat are the tall ones; every high thing is shamikh. ﴿And We gave you to drink sweet water (furat)﴾, that is, sweet water. Al-furat is sweet water from which one drinks and with which one irrigates.

Muqatil said: All of this is more wondrous than the resurrection.

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾, for the blessings We bestowed upon them, among Our blessings of which this is a part.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, related from Abu Hurayrah regarding ﴿And those sent forth in succession (al-mursalat 'urfa)﴾ that he said: They are the angels, sent with goodness (al-'urf).

Ibn Jarir related the same from Ibn Mas'ud.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿al-mursalat 'urfa﴾ that he said: the wind; ﴿fa'l-'asifat 'asfa﴾: the wind; ﴿wa'l-nashirat nashra﴾: the wind.

Ibn Rahawayh, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related that a man came to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and said: What are "al-'asifat 'asfa"? He said: The winds.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿al-mursalat 'urfa﴾ that he said: the wind; ﴿fa'l-'asifat 'asfa﴾: the wind; ﴿fa'l-fariqat farqa﴾: the angels; ﴿fa'l-mulqiyat dhikra﴾: the angels.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from him regarding ﴿al-mursalat 'urfa﴾ that he said: the angels; ﴿fa'l-fariqat farqa﴾: the angels, who separated truth from falsehood; ﴿fa'l-mulqiyat dhikra﴾: with the revelation.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "Woe" (wayl) is a valley in Hell in which the pus of the people of the Fire flows, and it was made for the deniers.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿minma'in mahin﴾ that he said: weak.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding kifatan that he said: a shelter (kinnan).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also regarding ﴿rawasi shamikhat﴾ that he said: towering mountains; and regarding His saying "furatan" that he said: sweet.

**Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, on Surah al-Mursalat (77), verses 29–50**

﴿Inṭalaqū ilā mā kuntum﴾ is governed by an implied verb of speech (*taqdir al-qawl*), meaning: it is said to them, as rebuke and reproach. ﴿Inṭalaqū ilā mā kuntum bihi tukadhdhibūn﴾ ("Go to that which you used to deny") in the world. The keepers of Hell (*khazanat Jahannam*) say this to them. That is: proceed to the punishment you used to deny, which is the punishment of the Fire. ﴿Inṭalaqū ilā ẓillin dhī thalāth shuʿab﴾ ("Go to a shade with three branches"): that is, to a shade of the smoke of Hell which has risen and then split into three columns, in which you will remain until the reckoning is finished. This is the nature of a great smoke: when it rises, it branches into divisions.

The majority of readers (*al-Jumhur*) read *inṭalaqū* in both places in the imperative form, for emphasis.

Ruways, on the authority of Yaʿqub, read the second occurrence in the past tense (*al-māḍī*): that is, when they were commanded to set out, they complied and set out.

It has also been said that the "shade" here means the *surādiq* (the enclosing tent), which is a tongue of fire that surrounds them. It then divides into three branches and shades them until the reckoning of them is finished; after that they go on to the Fire.

It has also been said that it is the shade of *yaḥmūm* (black smoke), as in His words: ﴿in scorching wind and boiling water and a shade of black smoke﴾, as has already been mentioned.

Then Allah, glorified is He, described this shade, mocking them, saying: ﴿Neither cool nor protective against the blaze﴾: that is, it gives no shade from the heat and does not protect against the flame.

Al-Kalbi said: it does not turn away the heat of Hell from you.

Then He described the Fire, saying: ﴿Indeed, it throws up sparks like a *qaṣr*﴾: that is, each spark it throws is as large as one of the great palaces (*quṣūr*). *Sharar* is what flies off from the fire scattered in pieces, and *qaṣr* is a great building.

It has also been said that *qaṣr* is the plural of *qaṣrah* (with a silent ṣād), like *ḥumr* and *ḥumrah*, or *tamr* and *tamrah*, and that it means a single piece of thick, heavy firewood.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: they are the large roots of trees. It has also been said that they are their necks (*aʿnāquhu*).

The majority read *ka-l-qaṣr* with a silent ṣād (*bi-iskān al-ṣād*), which is the singular of *quṣūr*, as already mentioned. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Ḥumayd and al-Sulami read it with a vowelled ṣād (*bi-fatḥ al-ṣād*), meaning the necks of palm trees. The word *qaṣarah* means "neck", and its plural is *qaṣr* and *qaṣarāt*.

Qatadah said: the necks of camels.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr read it with a kasra on the qāf and a fatḥa on the ṣād, which is also a plural of *qaṣrah*, like *badr* and *badrah*, or *qaṣʿ* and *qaṣʿah*.

The majority read *bi-sharar* with a fatḥa on the shīn. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Miqsam read it with a kasra on the shīn and an alif between the two rāʾs. ʿIsa read it likewise, except with a fatḥa on the shīn. These are different dialects (*lughāt*).

Then He likened the sparks in respect of their colour, saying: ﴿As if they were yellow camels (*jimālatun ṣufr*)﴾. *Jimālah* is a plural of *jimāl*, which means camels, or a plural of *jammālah* (a rope-maker's cable).

The majority read *jimālāt* with a kasra on the jīm. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾi and Ḥafṣ read *jimālah* as the plural of *jamal* (camel). Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah and Abu Rajaʾ read *jumālāt* with a ḍamma on the jīm, meaning ship-ropes (*ḥibāl al-sufun*).

Al-Wahidi said: the word *ṣufr* means "black" in the view of the exegetes (*al-mufassirūn*).

Al-Farrāʾ said: *ṣufr* means the blackness of camels. No black camel is seen without a tinge of yellow in it, and for that reason the Arabs called black camels *ṣufr*.

It has been said that when sparks fly off and fall, and have something of the colour of fire in them, they most resemble black camels. From this is the saying of the poet:

*Those are my horses and those are my mounts; they are yellow, and their young are like raisins.*

That is, they are black.

It has been said that this view is impossible in the language, since a thing cannot have a small admixture of something else and then be entirely attributed to that admixture. How strange is the one who says this, when Allah, the Exalted, has said: ﴿jimālatun ṣufr﴾.

It has been answered that its meaning is this: the Fire was created from light, so it is bright. When Allah created Jahannam, which is the place of the Fire, He filled that place with that fire, and sent to it His authority and His wrath. It became black from His authority, grew blacker, and became blacker than anything else. Thus its sparks are black, because they come from black fire.

I say: this answer does not refute what the objector said, because his statement, in terms of what occurs in the Noble Book here, describes the Fire as yellow. If the matter were as the answerer stated, namely that the Fire and its sparks are black, Allah would have said: "as if they were black camels." However, since the Arabs call black things *aṣfar* (yellow), there is no problem left, for the Qur'an was revealed in their language, and trustworthy authorities have transmitted that usage from them. So what is in the Qur'an here follows this Arabic usage.

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾ of the messengers of Allah and His signs.

﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾: that is, they will not talk. Al-Wahidi said: the exegetes said that the Day of Resurrection has stations (*mawāqif*); in some of them they speak, and in some of them a seal is placed on their mouths so that they do not speak. We have already mentioned this way of reconciling the verses in more than one place.

It has also been said that this refers to the time of their entry into the Fire, when they will not speak, because the stations of questioning and reckoning will have ended.

Al-Ḥasan said: they will not speak with any proof, even though they will be speaking.

The majority read *yawmun* with a ḍamma (*rafʿ*), as the predicate of the demonstrative (*ism al-ishārah*). Zayd ibn ʿAli, al-Aʿraj, al-Aʿmash, Abu Ḥayah, and ʿĀṣim in one transmission from him read it with a fatḥa, because it is built (*bināʾ*) on the fatḥa due to its being attached to a verb. Its position is in the nominative as predicate. It has also been said that it is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*ẓarf*). The demonstrative *hādhā* refers to the threat mentioned earlier, as if it were said: this punishment mentioned is due on the day when they will not speak.

﴿Nor will they be permitted to offer excuses﴾. The majority read *yu’dhanu* in the passive voice. Zayd ibn ʿAli read *lā yaʾdhanu* in the active voice, meaning: Allah will not permit them, that is, they will have no permission from Allah, so they will have no excuse, without making the excuse a consequence of permission, as would be the case if the verb were in the subjunctive (*naṣb*).

Al-Farrāʾ said: the *fāʾ* in *fa-yaʿtadhirūn* is coordinated with *yu’dhanu*. This is permitted because the endings of the discourse are in *nūn*. If he had said *fa-yaʿtadhirū* it would not have matched the verse-endings. He has also said: ﴿It will not be decreed upon them so that they die﴾ [Fāṭir 35:36], with the subjunctive, and both are correct.

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾, for what the messengers called them to and warned them of its consequence.

﴿This is the Day of Decision; We have gathered you and the former peoples﴾: that is, it is said to them: this is the Day of Decision, on which judgment is passed among creatures and truth is distinguished from falsehood. The address in *jamaʿnākum* is to the disbelievers of the time of our Prophet Muḥammad (ﷺ), and by "the former ones" is meant the disbelievers of earlier nations.

﴿So if you have a scheme﴾: that is, if you are able to devise a scheme now, then devise it against Me. This is rebuke and reproach for them.

Muqatil said: he means, if you have a stratagem, then employ it for yourselves. It has also been said that the meaning is: if you are able to wage war, then wage it. It has also been said that this is the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ), and so it is like the words of Hud: ﴿So plot against me all together, and give me no respite﴾ [Hud 11:55].

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾, because their helplessness and the falsity of what they held in the world became manifest to them.

Then Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the believers, saying: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in shades and springs﴾: that is, in the shade of trees and the shade of palaces, unlike the shade of the disbelievers, which is of smoke or of fire, as has already been mentioned.

Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: by "the God-fearing" is meant those who guard against associating partners with Allah, because the whole surah, from beginning to end, is a rebuke of the disbelievers for their disbelief.

Al-Razi said: this verse must be mentioned for this purpose, otherwise the surah would fall apart in its composition and order. The composition is only complete if the promise to the believers is made because of their faith; but making it a cause of obedience does not fit the composition. So he said. By "springs" are meant rivers, and by "fruits" what they take delight in, from what their souls desire and their appetites call for.

﴿Eat and drink with ease for what you used to do﴾: that is, it is said to them. The clause is implicitly introduced by *qawl*, and it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of the God-fearing. The *bāʾ* is causal (*sababiyyah*): that is, because of what you used to do in the world of good deeds.

﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers﴾: that is, by a reward like this great one, We reward the good-doers for their deeds. The majority read *fī ẓilāl* (in shades). Al-Aʿmash, al-Zuhri, Ṭalḥah and al-Aʿraj read *fī ẓulul*, the plural of *ẓullah*.

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾, since they are in great misery, while the believers are in lasting bliss.

﴿Eat and enjoy yourselves a little; indeed you are criminals﴾: the clause is implicitly introduced by *qawl* and is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state of the deniers. That is: woe is established for them at the time when this is said to them, as a reminder of their state in the world. Or it is said to them this in the world. The *mujrimūn* are those who associate partners with Allah. Although this is in form an imperative, in meaning it is a threat and a severe warning.

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾: He repeated it to increase the rebuke and reproach.

﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down﴾: that is, when they are commanded to pray, they do not pray.

Muqatil said: this was revealed concerning the tribe of Thaqīf, who refused to pray after the Prophet (ﷺ) had commanded them to. They said: "We will not bow, for it is a disgrace upon us." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no good in a religion that has no bowing or prostration in it."

It has also been said that this is said to them only in the Hereafter, when they are called to prostrate and cannot.

It has also been said that by bowing is meant obedience and humility.

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾ of the commands and prohibitions of Allah, glorified is He.

﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾: that is, in what statement after the Qur'an will they believe, if they do not believe in it?

The majority read *yu'minūn* with the *yāʾ* (third person, *ghaybah*). Ibn ʿĀmir in one transmission from him, and Yaʿqub, read it with the *tāʾ* (second person, *khiṭāb*).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His words ﴿like a qaṣr with sparks﴾, that he said: like a great palace. And concerning His words ﴿yellow camels﴾, he said: pieces of copper.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Hannad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ḥakim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted by way of ʿAbd al-Raḥman ibn ʿAbis, who said: I heard Ibn ʿAbbas being asked about His words: ﴿Indeed it throws sparks like a qaṣr﴾, and he said: We used to take a piece of wood of three cubits or less, and we would raise it for the winter, and we called it the *qaṣr*.

He said: I heard him being asked about His words: ﴿yellow camels﴾, and he said: they are ship-ropes, joined one to another until they are like men's waists.

The wording of al-Bukhari is: We used to take a piece of wood three cubits long or more and raise it for the winter, and we called it the *qaṣr*. ﴿As if they were yellow camels﴾: ship-ropes, joined together until they are like men's waists.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him that he read *ka-l-qaṣar* with a fatḥa on the qāf and the ṣād. He said: *qaṣar al-nakhl*, meaning the necks.

Ibn Mardawayh also transmitted from him that he said: the Arabs in the Jāhiliyyah used to say, "Cut us wood (*aqṣirū lanā al-ḥaṭab*)," and it would be cut to the size of a cubit or two cubits.

Saʿid ibn Manṣur, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥatim and al-Ṭabarani in *al-Awsaṭ* transmitted from Ibn Masʿud, concerning His words: ﴿It throws sparks like a qaṣr﴾, that he said: it is not like trees and mountains, but like cities and fortresses.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His words "like a qaṣr", that he said: it is the palace (*al-qaṣr*). And concerning His words "yellow camels", he said: the camels.

al-Ḥakim, and he authenticated it, transmitted by way of ʿIkrimah, who said: Nafiʿ ibn al-Azraq asked Ibn ʿAbbas about His words: ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾, ﴿Then not a sound will you hear except a whisper﴾, ﴿And some of them will turn to others, questioning one another﴾, and ﴿Here, read my record!﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah 69:19]. Ibn ʿAbbas said to him: Woe to you! Have you asked about this of anyone before me? He said: No. He said: If you had asked, you would have been destroyed. Did not Allah say: ﴿Indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾ [al-Ḥajj 22:47]? He said: Yes. He said: Then for each measure of a day of these days there is a colour of colours.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His words: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down﴾, that he said: they will be called on the Day of Resurrection to prostrate and will be unable to, because in the world they did not prostrate to Allah.

**Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, on Surah al-Mursalat (77), verses 29–50**

The keepers of Hell (*khazanat Jahannam*) say this to them. That is: proceed to the punishment you used to deny, which is the punishment of the Fire. ﴿Inṭalaqū ilā ẓillin dhī thalāth shuʿab﴾ ("Go to a shade with three branches"): that is, to a shade of the smoke of Hell which has risen and then split into three columns, in which you will remain until the reckoning is finished. This is the nature of a great smoke: when it rises, it branches into divisions.

The majority of readers (*al-Jumhur*) read *inṭalaqū* in both places in the imperative form, for emphasis.

Ruways, on the authority of Yaʿqub, read the second occurrence in the past tense (*al-māḍī*): that is, when they were commanded to set out, they complied and set out.

It has also been said that the "shade" here means the *surādiq* (the enclosing tent), which is a tongue of fire that surrounds them. It then divides into three branches and shades them until the reckoning of them is finished; after that they go on to the Fire.

It has also been said that it is the shade of *yaḥmūm* (black smoke), as in His words: ﴿in scorching wind and boiling water and a shade of black smoke﴾, as has already been mentioned.

Then Allah, glorified is He, described this shade, mocking them, saying: ﴿Neither cool nor protective against the blaze﴾: that is, it gives no shade from the heat and does not protect against the flame.

He said: I heard him being asked about His words: ﴿yellow camels﴾, and he said: they are ship-ropes, joined one to another until they are like men's waists.

al-Ḥakim, and he authenticated it, transmitted by way of ʿIkrimah, who said: Nafiʿ ibn al-Azraq asked Ibn ʿAbbas about His words: ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾, ﴿Then not a sound will you hear except a whisper﴾, ﴿And some of them will turn to others, questioning one another﴾, and ﴿Here, read my record!﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah 69:19]. **Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, on Surah al-Mursalat (77), verses 29–50**

﴿Inṭalaqū ilā mā kuntum﴾ is governed by an implied verb of speech (*taqdir al-qawl*), meaning: it is said to them, as rebuke and reproach. ﴿Inṭalaqū ilā mā kuntum bihi tukadhdhibūn﴾ ("Go to that which you used to deny") in the world. The keepers of Hell (*khazanat Jahannam*) say this to them. That is: proceed to the punishment you used to deny, which is the punishment of the Fire. ﴿Inṭalaqū ilā ẓillin dhī thalāth shuʿab﴾ ("Go to a shade with three branches"): that is, to a shade of the smoke of Hell which has risen and then split into three columns, in which you will remain until the reckoning is finished. This is the nature of a great smoke: when it rises, it branches into divisions.

The majority of readers (*al-Jumhur*) read *inṭalaqū* in both places in the imperative form, for emphasis.

Ruways, on the authority of Yaʿqub, read the second occurrence in the past tense (*al-māḍī*): that is, when they were commanded to set out, they complied and set out.

It has also been said that the "shade" here means the *surādiq* (the enclosing tent), which is a tongue of fire that surrounds them. It then divides into three branches and shades them until the reckoning of them is finished; after that they go on to the Fire.

It has also been said that it is the shade of *yaḥmūm* (black smoke), as in His words: ﴿in scorching wind and boiling water and a shade of black smoke﴾, as has already been mentioned.

Then Allah, glorified is He, described this shade, mocking them, saying: ﴿Neither cool nor protective against the blaze﴾: that is, it gives no shade from the heat and does not protect against the flame.

Al-Kalbi said: it does not turn away the heat of Hell from you.

Then He described the Fire, saying: ﴿Indeed, it throws up sparks like a *qaṣr*﴾: that is, each spark it throws is as large as one of the great palaces (*quṣūr*). *Sharar* is what flies off from the fire scattered in pieces, and *qaṣr* is a great building.

It has also been said that *qaṣr* is the plural of *qaṣrah* (with a silent ṣād), like *ḥumr* and *ḥumrah*, or *tamr* and *tamrah*, and that it means a single piece of thick, heavy firewood.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: they are the large roots of trees. It has also been said that they are their necks (*aʿnāquhu*).

The majority read *ka-l-qaṣr* with a silent ṣād (*bi-iskān al-ṣād*), which is the singular of *quṣūr*, as already mentioned. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Ḥumayd and al-Sulami read it with a vowelled ṣād (*bi-fatḥ al-ṣād*), meaning the necks of palm trees. The word *qaṣarah* means "neck", and its plural is *qaṣr* and *qaṣarāt*.

Qatadah said: the necks of camels.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr read it with a kasra on the qāf and a fatḥa on the ṣād, which is also a plural of *qaṣrah*, like *badr* and *badrah*, or *qaṣʿ* and *qaṣʿah*.

The majority read *bi-sharar* with a fatḥa on the shīn. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Miqsam read it with a kasra on the shīn and an alif between the two rāʾs. ʿIsa read it likewise, except with a fatḥa on the shīn. These are different dialects (*lughāt*).

Then He likened the sparks in respect of their colour, saying: ﴿As if they were yellow camels (*jimālatun ṣufr*)﴾. *Jimālah* is a plural of *jimāl*, which means camels, or a plural of *jammālah* (a rope-maker's cable).

The majority read *jimālāt* with a kasra on the jīm. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾi and Ḥafṣ read *jimālah* as the plural of *jamal* (camel). Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah and Abu Rajaʾ read *jumālāt* with a ḍamma on the jīm, meaning ship-ropes (*ḥibāl al-sufun*).

Al-Wahidi said: the word *ṣufr* means "black" in the view of the exegetes (*al-mufassirūn*).

Al-Farrāʾ said: *ṣufr* means the blackness of camels. No black camel is seen without a tinge of yellow in it, and for that reason the Arabs called black camels *ṣufr*.

It has been said that when sparks fly off and fall, and have something of the colour of fire in them, they most resemble black camels. From this is the saying of the poet:

*Those are my horses and those are my mounts; they are yellow, and their young are like raisins.*

That is, they are black.

It has been said that this view is impossible in the language, since a thing cannot have a small admixture of something else and then be entirely attributed to that admixture. How strange is the one who says this, when Allah, the Exalted, has said: ﴿jimālatun ṣufr﴾.

It has been answered that its meaning is this: the Fire was created from light, so it is bright. When Allah created Jahannam, which is the place of the Fire, He filled that place with that fire, and sent to it His authority and His wrath. It became black from His authority, grew blacker, and became blacker than anything else. Thus its sparks are black, because they come from black fire.

I say: this answer does not refute what the objector said, because his statement, in terms of what occurs in the Noble Book here, describes the Fire as yellow. If the matter were as the answerer stated, namely that the Fire and its sparks are black, Allah would have said: "as if they were black camels." However, since the Arabs call black things *aṣfar* (yellow), there is no problem left, for the Qur'an was revealed in their language, and trustworthy authorities have transmitted that usage from them. So what is in the Qur'an here follows this Arabic usage.

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾ of the messengers of Allah and His signs.

﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾: that is, they will not talk. Al-Wahidi said: the exegetes said that the Day of Resurrection has stations (*mawāqif*); in some of them they speak, and in some of them a seal is placed on their mouths so that they do not speak. We have already mentioned this way of reconciling the verses in more than one place.

It has also been said that this refers to the time of their entry into the Fire, when they will not speak, because the stations of questioning and reckoning will have ended.

Al-Ḥasan said: they will not speak with any proof, even though they will be speaking.

The majority read *yawmun* with a ḍamma (*rafʿ*), as the predicate of the demonstrative (*ism al-ishārah*). Zayd ibn ʿAli, al-Aʿraj, al-Aʿmash, Abu Ḥayah, and ʿĀṣim in one transmission from him read it with a fatḥa, because it is built (*bināʾ*) on the fatḥa due to its being attached to a verb. Its position is in the nominative as predicate. It has also been said that it is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*ẓarf*). The demonstrative *hādhā* refers to the threat mentioned earlier, as if it were said: this punishment mentioned is due on the day when they will not speak.

﴿Nor will they be permitted to offer excuses﴾. The majority read *yu’dhanu* in the passive voice. Zayd ibn ʿAli read *lā yaʾdhanu* in the active voice, meaning: Allah will not permit them, that is, they will have no permission from Allah, so they will have no excuse, without making the excuse a consequence of permission, as would be the case if the verb were in the subjunctive (*naṣb*).

Al-Farrāʾ said: the *fāʾ* in *fa-yaʿtadhirūn* is coordinated with *yu’dhanu*. This is permitted because the endings of the discourse are in *nūn*. If he had said *fa-yaʿtadhirū* it would not have matched the verse-endings. He has also said: ﴿It will not be decreed upon them so that they die﴾ [Fāṭir 35:36], with the subjunctive, and both are correct.

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾, for what the messengers called them to and warned them of its consequence.

﴿This is the Day of Decision; We have gathered you and the former peoples﴾: that is, it is said to them: this is the Day of Decision, on which judgment is passed among creatures and truth is distinguished from falsehood. The address in *jamaʿnākum* is to the disbelievers of the time of our Prophet Muḥammad (ﷺ), and by "the former ones" is meant the disbelievers of earlier nations.

﴿So if you have a scheme﴾: that is, if you are able to devise a scheme now, then devise it against Me. This is rebuke and reproach for them.

Muqatil said: he means, if you have a stratagem, then employ it for yourselves. It has also been said that the meaning is: if you are able to wage war, then wage it. It has also been said that this is the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ), and so it is like the words of Hud: ﴿So plot against me all together, and give me no respite﴾ [Hud 11:55].

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾, because their helplessness and the falsity of what they held in the world became manifest to them.

Then Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the believers, saying: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in shades and springs﴾: that is, in the shade of trees and the shade of palaces, unlike the shade of the disbelievers, which is of smoke or of fire, as has already been mentioned.

Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: by "the God-fearing" is meant those who guard against associating partners with Allah, because the whole surah, from beginning to end, is a rebuke of the disbelievers for their disbelief.

Al-Razi said: this verse must be mentioned for this purpose, otherwise the surah would fall apart in its composition and order. The composition is only complete if the promise to the believers is made because of their faith; but making it a cause of obedience does not fit the composition. So he said. By "springs" are meant rivers, and by "fruits" what they take delight in, from what their souls desire and their appetites call for.

﴿Eat and drink with ease for what you used to do﴾: that is, it is said to them. The clause is implicitly introduced by *qawl*, and it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of the God-fearing. The *bāʾ* is causal (*sababiyyah*): that is, because of what you used to do in the world of good deeds.

﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers﴾: that is, by a reward like this great one, We reward the good-doers for their deeds. The majority read *fī ẓilāl* (in shades). Al-Aʿmash, al-Zuhri, Ṭalḥah and al-Aʿraj read *fī ẓulul*, the plural of *ẓullah*.

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾, since they are in great misery, while the believers are in lasting bliss.

﴿Eat and enjoy yourselves a little; indeed you are criminals﴾: the clause is implicitly introduced by *qawl* and is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state of the deniers. That is: woe is established for them at the time when this is said to them, as a reminder of their state in the world. Or it is said to them this in the world. The *mujrimūn* are those who associate partners with Allah. Although this is in form an imperative, in meaning it is a threat and a severe warning.

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾: He repeated it to increase the rebuke and reproach.

﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down﴾: that is, when they are commanded to pray, they do not pray.

Muqatil said: this was revealed concerning the tribe of Thaqīf, who refused to pray after the Prophet (ﷺ) had commanded them to. They said: "We will not bow, for it is a disgrace upon us." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no good in a religion that has no bowing or prostration in it."

It has also been said that this is said to them only in the Hereafter, when they are called to prostrate and cannot.

It has also been said that by bowing is meant obedience and humility.

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾ of the commands and prohibitions of Allah, glorified is He.

﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾: that is, in what statement after the Qur'an will they believe, if they do not believe in it?

al-Ḥakim, and he authenticated it, transmitted by way of ʿIkrimah, who said: Nafiʿ ibn al-Azraq asked Ibn ʿAbbas about His words: ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾, ﴿Then not a sound will you hear except a whisper﴾, ﴿And some of them will turn to others, questioning one another﴾, and ﴿Here, read my record!﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah 69:19]. **Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, on Surah al-Mursalat (77), verses 29–50**

﴿Inṭalaqū ilā mā kuntum﴾ is governed by an implied verb of speech (*taqdir al-qawl*), meaning: it is said to them, as rebuke and reproach. ﴿Inṭalaqū ilā mā kuntum bihi tukadhdhibūn﴾ ("Go to that which you used to deny") in the world. The keepers of Hell (*khazanat Jahannam*) say this to them. That is: proceed to the punishment you used to deny, which is the punishment of the Fire. ﴿Inṭalaqū ilā ẓillin dhī thalāth shuʿab﴾ ("Go to a shade with three branches"): that is, to a shade of the smoke of Hell which has risen and then split into three columns, in which you will remain until the reckoning is finished. This is the nature of a great smoke: when it rises, it branches into divisions.

The majority of readers (*al-Jumhur*) read *inṭalaqū* in both places in the imperative form, for emphasis.

Ruways, on the authority of Yaʿqub, read the second occurrence in the past tense (*al-māḍī*): that is, when they were commanded to set out, they complied and set out.

It has also been said that the "shade" here means the *surādiq* (the enclosing tent), which is a tongue of fire that surrounds them. It then divides into three branches and shades them until the reckoning of them is finished; after that they go on to the Fire.

It has also been said that it is the shade of *yaḥmūm* (black smoke), as in His words: ﴿in scorching wind and boiling water and a shade of black smoke﴾, as has already been mentioned.

Then Allah, glorified is He, described this shade, mocking them, saying: ﴿Neither cool nor protective against the blaze﴾: that is, it gives no shade from the heat and does not protect against the flame.

Al-Kalbi said: it does not turn away the heat of Hell from you.

Then He described the Fire, saying: ﴿Indeed, it throws up sparks like a *qaṣr*﴾: that is, each spark it throws is as large as one of the great palaces (*quṣūr*). *Sharar* is what flies off from the fire scattered in pieces, and *qaṣr* is a great building.

It has also been said that *qaṣr* is the plural of *qaṣrah* (with a silent ṣād), like *ḥumr* and *ḥumrah*, or *tamr* and *tamrah*, and that it means a single piece of thick, heavy firewood.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: they are the large roots of trees. It has also been said that they are their necks (*aʿnāquhu*).

The majority read *ka-l-qaṣr* with a silent ṣād (*bi-iskān al-ṣād*), which is the singular of *quṣūr*, as already mentioned. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Ḥumayd and al-Sulami read it with a vowelled ṣād (*bi-fatḥ al-ṣād*), meaning the necks of palm trees. The word *qaṣarah* means "neck", and its plural is *qaṣr* and *qaṣarāt*.

Qatadah said: the necks of camels.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr read it with a kasra on the qāf and a fatḥa on the ṣād, which is also a plural of *qaṣrah*, like *badr* and *badrah*, or *qaṣʿ* and *qaṣʿah*.

The majority read *bi-sharar* with a fatḥa on the shīn. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Miqsam read it with a kasra on the shīn and an alif between the two rāʾs. ʿIsa read it likewise, except with a fatḥa on the shīn. These are different dialects (*lughāt*).

Then He likened the sparks in respect of their colour, saying: ﴿As if they were yellow camels (*jimālatun ṣufr*)﴾. *Jimālah* is a plural of *jimāl*, which means camels, or a plural of *jammālah* (a rope-maker's cable).

The majority read *jimālāt* with a kasra on the jīm. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾi and Ḥafṣ read *jimālah* as the plural of *jamal* (camel). Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah and Abu Rajaʾ read *jumālāt* with a ḍamma on the jīm, meaning ship-ropes (*ḥibāl al-sufun*).

Al-Wahidi said: the word *ṣufr* means "black" in the view of the exegetes (*al-mufassirūn*).

Al-Farrāʾ said: *ṣufr* means the blackness of camels. No black camel is seen without a tinge of yellow in it, and for that reason the Arabs called black camels *ṣufr*.

It has been said that when sparks fly off and fall, and have something of the colour of fire in them, they most resemble black camels. From this is the saying of the poet:

*Those are my horses and those are my mounts; they are yellow, and their young are like raisins.*

That is, they are black.

It has been said that this view is impossible in the language, since a thing cannot have a small admixture of something else and then be entirely attributed to that admixture. How strange is the one who says this, when Allah, the Exalted, has said: ﴿jimālatun ṣufr﴾.

It has been answered that its meaning is this: the Fire was created from light, so it is bright. When Allah created Jahannam, which is the place of the Fire, He filled that place with that fire, and sent to it His authority and His wrath. It became black from His authority, grew blacker, and became blacker than anything else. Thus its sparks are black, because they come from black fire.

I say: this answer does not refute what the objector said, because his statement, in terms of what occurs in the Noble Book here, describes the Fire as yellow. If the matter were as the answerer stated, namely that the Fire and its sparks are black, Allah would have said: "as if they were black camels." However, since the Arabs call black things *aṣfar* (yellow), there is no problem left, for the Qur'an was revealed in their language, and trustworthy authorities have transmitted that usage from them. So what is in the Qur'an here follows this Arabic usage.

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾ of the messengers of Allah and His signs.

﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾: that is, they will not talk. Al-Wahidi said: the exegetes said that the Day of Resurrection has stations (*mawāqif*); in some of them they speak, and in some of them a seal is placed on their mouths so that they do not speak. We have already mentioned this way of reconciling the verses in more than one place.

It has also been said that this refers to the time of their entry into the Fire, when they will not speak, because the stations of questioning and reckoning will have ended.

Al-Ḥasan said: they will not speak with any proof, even though they will be speaking.

The majority read *yawmun* with a ḍamma (*rafʿ*), as the predicate of the demonstrative (*ism al-ishārah*). Zayd ibn ʿAli, al-Aʿraj, al-Aʿmash, Abu Ḥayah, and ʿĀṣim in one transmission from him read it with a fatḥa, because it is built (*bināʾ*) on the fatḥa due to its being attached to a verb. Its position is in the nominative as predicate. It has also been said that it is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*ẓarf*). The demonstrative *hādhā* refers to the threat mentioned earlier, as if it were said: this punishment mentioned is due on the day when they will not speak.

﴿Nor will they be permitted to offer excuses﴾. The majority read *yu’dhanu* in the passive voice. Zayd ibn ʿAli read *lā yaʾdhanu* in the active voice, meaning: Allah will not permit them, that is, they will have no permission from Allah, so they will have no excuse, without making the excuse a consequence of permission, as would be the case if the verb were in the subjunctive (*naṣb*).

Al-Farrāʾ said: the *fāʾ* in *fa-yaʿtadhirūn* is coordinated with *yu’dhanu*. This is permitted because the endings of the discourse are in *nūn*. If he had said *fa-yaʿtadhirū* it would not have matched the verse-endings. He has also said: ﴿It will not be decreed upon them so that they die﴾ [Fāṭir 35:36], with the subjunctive, and both are correct.

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾, for what the messengers called them to and warned them of its consequence.

﴿This is the Day of Decision; We have gathered you and the former peoples﴾: that is, it is said to them: this is the Day of Decision, on which judgment is passed among creatures and truth is distinguished from falsehood. The address in *jamaʿnākum* is to the disbelievers of the time of our Prophet Muḥammad (ﷺ), and by "the former ones" is meant the disbelievers of earlier nations.

﴿So if you have a scheme﴾: that is, if you are able to devise a scheme now, then devise it against Me. This is rebuke and reproach for them.

Muqatil said: he means, if you have a stratagem, then employ it for yourselves. It has also been said that the meaning is: if you are able to wage war, then wage it. It has also been said that this is the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ), and so it is like the words of Hud: ﴿So plot against me all together, and give me no respite﴾ [Hud 11:55].

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾, because their helplessness and the falsity of what they held in the world became manifest to them.

Then Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the believers, saying: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in shades and springs﴾: that is, in the shade of trees and the shade of palaces, unlike the shade of the disbelievers, which is of smoke or of fire, as has already been mentioned.

Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: by "the God-fearing" is meant those who guard against associating partners with Allah, because the whole surah, from beginning to end, is a rebuke of the disbelievers for their disbelief.

Al-Razi said: this verse must be mentioned for this purpose, otherwise the surah would fall apart in its composition and order. The composition is only complete if the promise to the believers is made because of their faith; but making it a cause of obedience does not fit the composition. So he said. By "springs" are meant rivers, and by "fruits" what they take delight in, from what their souls desire and their appetites call for.

﴿Eat and drink with ease for what you used to do﴾: that is, it is said to them. The clause is implicitly introduced by *qawl*, and it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of the God-fearing. The *bāʾ* is causal (*sababiyyah*): that is, because of what you used to do in the world of good deeds.

﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers﴾: that is, by a reward like this great one, We reward the good-doers for their deeds. The majority read *fī ẓilāl* (in shades). Al-Aʿmash, al-Zuhri, Ṭalḥah and al-Aʿraj read *fī ẓulul*, the plural of *ẓullah*.

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾, since they are in great misery, while the believers are in lasting bliss.

﴿Eat and enjoy yourselves a little; indeed you are criminals﴾: the clause is implicitly introduced by *qawl* and is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state of the deniers. That is: woe is established for them at the time when this is said to them, as a reminder of their state in the world. Or it is said to them this in the world. The *mujrimūn* are those who associate partners with Allah. Although this is in form an imperative, in meaning it is a threat and a severe warning.

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾: He repeated it to increase the rebuke and reproach.

﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down﴾: that is, when they are commanded to pray, they do not pray.

Muqatil said: this was revealed concerning the tribe of Thaqīf, who refused to pray after the Prophet (ﷺ) had commanded them to. They said: "We will not bow, for it is a disgrace upon us." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no good in a religion that has no bowing or prostration in it."

It has also been said that this is said to them only in the Hereafter, when they are called to prostrate and cannot.

It has also been said that by bowing is meant obedience and humility.

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾ of the commands and prohibitions of Allah, glorified is He.

﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾: that is, in what statement after the Qur'an will they believe, if they do not believe in it?

The majority read *yu'minūn* with the *yāʾ* (third person, *ghaybah*). Ibn ʿĀmir in one transmission from him, and Yaʿqub, read it with the *tāʾ* (second person, *khiṭāb*).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His words ﴿like a qaṣr with sparks﴾, that he said: like a great palace. And concerning His words ﴿yellow camels﴾, he said: pieces of copper.

He said: I heard him being asked about His words: ﴿yellow camels﴾, and he said: they are ship-ropes, joined one to another until they are like men's waists.

The wording of al-Bukhari is: We used to take a piece of wood three cubits long or more and raise it for the winter, and we called it the *qaṣr*. ﴿As if they were yellow camels﴾: ship-ropes, joined together until they are like men's waists.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him that he read *ka-l-qaṣar* with a fatḥa on the qāf and the ṣād. He said: *qaṣar al-nakhl*, meaning the necks.

The majority of readers (*al-Jumhur*) read *inṭalaqū* in both places in the imperative form, for emphasis.

Ruways, on the authority of Yaʿqub, read the second occurrence in the past tense (*al-māḍī*): that is, when they were commanded to set out, they complied and set out.

It has also been said that it is the shade of *yaḥmūm* (black smoke), as in His words: ﴿in scorching wind and boiling water and a shade of black smoke﴾, as has already been mentioned.

Al-Kalbi said: it does not turn away the heat of Hell from you.

It has also been said that *qaṣr* is the plural of *qaṣrah* (with a silent ṣād), like *ḥumr* and *ḥumrah*, or *tamr* and *tamrah*, and that it means a single piece of thick, heavy firewood.

Qatadah said: the necks of camels.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr read it with a kasra on the qāf and a fatḥa on the ṣād, which is also a plural of *qaṣrah*, like *badr* and *badrah*, or *qaṣʿ* and *qaṣʿah*.

The majority read *bi-sharar* with a fatḥa on the shīn. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Miqsam read it with a kasra on the shīn and an alif between the two rāʾs. ʿIsa read it likewise, except with a fatḥa on the shīn. These are different dialects (*lughāt*).

Then He likened the sparks in respect of their colour, saying: ﴿As if they were yellow camels (*jimālatun ṣufr*)﴾. *Jimālah* is a plural of *jimāl*, which means camels, or a plural of *jammālah* (a rope-maker's cable).

The clause is implicitly introduced by *qawl*, and it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of the God-fearing. The *bāʾ* is causal (*sababiyyah*): that is, because of what you used to do in the world of good deeds.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Hannad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ḥakim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted by way of ʿAbd al-Raḥman ibn ʿAbis, who said: I heard Ibn ʿAbbas being asked about His words: ﴿Indeed it throws sparks like a qaṣr﴾, and he said: We used to take a piece of wood of three cubits or less, and we would raise it for the winter, and we called it the *qaṣr*.

He said: I heard him being asked about His words: ﴿yellow camels﴾, and he said: they are ship-ropes, joined one to another until they are like men's waists.

The wording of al-Bukhari is: We used to take a piece of wood three cubits long or more and raise it for the winter, and we called it the *qaṣr*. ﴿As if they were yellow camels﴾: ship-ropes, joined together until they are like men's waists.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His words "like a qaṣr", that he said: it is the palace (*al-qaṣr*). And concerning His words "yellow camels", he said: the camels.

al-Ḥakim, and he authenticated it, transmitted by way of ʿIkrimah, who said: Nafiʿ ibn al-Azraq asked Ibn ʿAbbas about His words: ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾, ﴿Then not a sound will you hear except a whisper﴾, ﴿And some of them will turn to others, questioning one another﴾, and ﴿Here, read my record!﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah 69:19]. Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His words: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down﴾, that he said: they will be called on the Day of Resurrection to prostrate and will be unable to, because in the world they did not prostrate to Allah.

Muqatil said: he means, if you have a stratagem, then employ it for yourselves. It has also been said that the meaning is: if you are able to wage war, then wage it. Then Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the believers, saying: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in shades and springs﴾: that is, in the shade of trees and the shade of palaces, unlike the shade of the disbelievers, which is of smoke or of fire, as has already been mentioned.

The composition is only complete if the promise to the believers is made because of their faith; but making it a cause of obedience does not fit the composition. So he said. By "springs" are meant rivers, and by "fruits" what they take delight in, from what their souls desire and their appetites call for.

The clause is implicitly introduced by *qawl*, and it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of the God-fearing. The *bāʾ* is causal (*sababiyyah*): that is, because of what you used to do in the world of good deeds.

It has also been said that by bowing is meant obedience and humility.

Then He likened the sparks in respect of their colour, saying: ﴿As if they were yellow camels (*jimālatun ṣufr*)﴾. *Jimālah* is a plural of *jimāl*, which means camels, or a plural of *jammālah* (a rope-maker's cable).

The majority read *jimālāt* with a kasra on the jīm. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾi and Ḥafṣ read *jimālah* as the plural of *jamal* (camel). Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah and Abu Rajaʾ read *jumālāt* with a ḍamma on the jīm, meaning ship-ropes (*ḥibāl al-sufun*).

It has been said that when sparks fly off and fall, and have something of the colour of fire in them, they most resemble black camels. From this is the saying of the poet:

*Those are my horses and those are my mounts; they are yellow, and their young are like raisins.*

That is, they are black.

It has been said that this view is impossible in the language, since a thing cannot have a small admixture of something else and then be entirely attributed to that admixture. How strange is the one who says this, when Allah, the Exalted, has said: ﴿jimālatun ṣufr﴾.

It has been answered that its meaning is this: the Fire was created from light, so it is bright. When Allah created Jahannam, which is the place of the Fire, He filled that place with that fire, and sent to it His authority and His wrath. I say: this answer does not refute what the objector said, because his statement, in terms of what occurs in the Noble Book here, describes the Fire as yellow. If the matter were as the answerer stated, namely that the Fire and its sparks are black, Allah would have said: "as if they were black camels." However, since the Arabs call black things *aṣfar* (yellow), there is no problem left, for the Qur'an was revealed in their language, and trustworthy authorities have transmitted that usage from them. So what is in the Qur'an here follows this Arabic usage.

The clause is implicitly introduced by *qawl*, and it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of the God-fearing. The *bāʾ* is causal (*sababiyyah*): that is, because of what you used to do in the world of good deeds.

He said: I heard him being asked about His words: ﴿yellow camels﴾, and he said: they are ship-ropes, joined one to another until they are like men's waists.

The wording of al-Bukhari is: We used to take a piece of wood three cubits long or more and raise it for the winter, and we called it the *qaṣr*. ﴿As if they were yellow camels﴾: ship-ropes, joined together until they are like men's waists.

al-Ḥakim, and he authenticated it, transmitted by way of ʿIkrimah, who said: Nafiʿ ibn al-Azraq asked Ibn ʿAbbas about His words: ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾, ﴿Then not a sound will you hear except a whisper﴾, ﴿And some of them will turn to others, questioning one another﴾, and ﴿Here, read my record!﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah 69:19].
